welcome.title: Welcome, Explorer!
welcome.pari_tip: There are no wrong ideas in this workbook. Try your best, ask questions, and have fun learning about AI!

syllabus.objective: I can identify features, labels and predictions.
I can tell regression and classification apart.
I can build a simple decision tree from data.
I can read a confusion matrix and calculate accuracy.
I can use lists, loops and if statements in Python.
I can explain neurons, weights and layers.
I can identify intents and entities.
I can explain fairness and accountability in AI.

units.title: How Machine Learning Works
learn_paragraphs:
Machine learning finds a pattern that links features (inputs) to a label (output).
Example: features = size, location, rooms → label = house price. The learned pattern
is the model.
When the model sees new features, it makes a prediction. Training adjusts the model
to make fewer errors.

predicting a category

units.title: Regression and Classification
learn_paragraphs:
Regression predicts a number: price, temperature, marks.
Classification predicts a category: spam/not spam, cat/dog, pass/fail.
A simple regression draws a line of best fit through data points to predict new
values.

new_words.definition: a table of right and wrong predictions
a key detail like a place or date
easy for people to understand why

units.title: Decision Trees from Data
learn_paragraphs:
A decision tree model learns questions from data that best separate the classes.
Each question splits the data. A good split makes groups that are as pure as possible
(mostly one class).
Trees are easy to explain: you can follow the path to see why a prediction was made.

units.title: Evaluating Models
learn_paragraphs:
A confusion matrix compares predictions with the truth: True Positive (TP), True
Negative (TN), False Positive (FP) and False Negative (FN).
Accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ total.
Accuracy can mislead. If 95 of 100 emails are not spam, a model that says “not
spam” every time is 95% accurate but useless.

units.did_you_know: In medical tests, a false negative can be more dangerous than a false positive.

units.title: Python: Lists, Loops and If
learn_paragraphs:
A list stores many values: marks = [72, 88, 95] .
A for loop repeats code for each item. An if statement makes decisions.
Together they let us process whole datasets, which is the heart of AI programming.

units.title: Neural Networks
learn_paragraphs:
A neural network is inspired by the brain. It has layers of artificial neurons: input,
hidden and output.
Each neuron multiplies inputs by weights, adds them up, and passes the result on if it
is strong enough.
Training adjusts the weights to reduce errors. Deep learning uses networks with
many hidden layers.

new_words.definition: a group of neurons
the final answer at the end of a branch
a line that follows the trend in data

units.did_you_know: Deep learning helped make big leaps in image recognition from around 2012.

units.title: Conversational AI
learn_paragraphs:
Chatbots find the user's intent (what they want) and entities (important details).
In “Book a train to Pune tomorrow”, intent = book_ticket, entities = Pune, tomorrow.
Rule-based bots follow scripts. AI chatbots learn from examples and handle many
ways of asking.

new_words.definition: an ordered collection of values
a unit that combines inputs
the model's output for new data

units.did_you_know: Many banks and railways use chatbots to answer common customer questions any time of day.
units.think_and_talk: Should a chatbot always tell users that it is not a human? Why?

units.title: Fairness and Accountability
learn_paragraphs:
AI decisions can affect jobs, loans and grades, so they must be fair and accountable.
Accountability means a person or organisation is responsible for what the AI does.
Good practice: test on different groups, explain decisions, allow people to appeal,
and keep a human in the loop.

dividing data using a question
how important an input is

units.did_you_know: Some AI laws require that people can get a human to review important automated decisions.
